current_example.title: Example: Identifying an Integral Expression For the Area of a Petal of a General Polar Curve

q-125494.name: Question 1
q-125494.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/a010feba178f2db834e1939a91c81fd95131d65b10c7616bd92140fa46eaa305.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-125494.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $7\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
7\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{7}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{7}].$ Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /7}{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-125494.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=6sin⁡(7θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
92∫0π/7sin2⁡(7θ)dθ
b
12∫0π/2sin2⁡(7θ)dθ
c
9∫0πsin2⁡(7θ)dθ
d
18∫0π/7sin2⁡(7θ)dθ
e
32∫0π/2sin2⁡(7θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=6sin⁡(7θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(6sin⁡(7θ))2dθ=18∫θ1θ2sin2⁡(7θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 6sin⁡(7θ)=0.

This gives us two solutions for 7θ∈[0,2π):

7θ=0,π⟹θ=0,π7

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[0,π7]. Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

A=18∫0π/7sin2⁡(7θ)dθ.

q-124424.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/97b30cfa241a6e1b9db4d5332749ae503a926711c0e7c78ab188c2327463c89b.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-124424.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
3\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $5\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
5\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{5}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{5}].$ Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}{sin}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-124424.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(5θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
32∫02π/5sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
34∫0π/10sin2⁡(5+θ)dθ
c
92∫0π/5sin2⁡(5θ)dθ
d
32∫0π/5sin⁡(5θ)dθ
e
92∫02π/5sin2⁡(θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=3sin⁡(5θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(3sin⁡(5θ))2dθ=92∫θ1θ2sin2⁡(5θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 3sin⁡(5θ)=0.

This gives us two solutions for 5θ∈[0,2π):

5θ=0,π⟹θ=0,π5

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[0,π5]. Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

A=92∫0π/5sin2⁡(5θ)dθ.

q-127796.name: Question 3
q-127796.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/192007bbd5aee67607897bc1e4e3e29d106c8f6041fe8b06025f48999e68fcfb.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-127796.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(9\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $9\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
9\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{9}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{9}].$  Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /9}{sin}^{2}⁡(9\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-127796.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=sin⁡(9θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
12∫0π/6sin2⁡(9θ)dθ
b
32∫0π/9sin2⁡(9θ)dθ
c
32∫0π/3sin2⁡(9θ)dθ
d
12∫0π/9sin2⁡(9θ)dθ
e
3∫0π/9sin2⁡(9θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=sin⁡(9θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(sin⁡(9θ))2dθ=12∫θ1θ2sin2⁡(9θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or sin⁡(9θ)=0. This gives us two solutions for 9θ∈[0,2π):

9θ=0,π⟹θ=0,π9

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[0,π9]. Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

A=12∫0π/9sin2⁡(9θ)dθ.

q-20905.name: Question 4
q-20905.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/01a371be4c5a555b0d3790431111468acfed1471d16c4c4c305bcfe311ce3576.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-20905.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $3\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
3\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{3}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{3}].$ Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-20905.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=sin⁡(3θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
2∫0π/4sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
b
12∫0π/4sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
12∫0π/3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
d
12∫−π/3π/3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
2∫0π/3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=sin⁡(3θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(sin⁡(3θ))2dθ=12∫θ1θ2sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or sin⁡(3θ)=0.

This gives us two solutions for 3θ∈[0,2π):

3θ=0,π⟹θ=0,π3

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[0,π3]. Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

A=12∫0π/3sin2⁡(3θ)dθ.

q-127794.name: Question 5
q-127794.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/b7475f0a169e62121711d52daaf51e8954053fc35738266d94240b6e70de6258.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-127794.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits.  

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=0.
$$

This gives us two solutions for $2\theta \in [0,2\pi ):$

$$
2\theta =0,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =0,\frac{\pi }{2}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$ Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
A=8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-127794.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=4sin⁡(2θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
4∫0π/2sin⁡(2θ)dθ
b
8∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
c
8∫0πsin2⁡(2θ)dθ
d
16∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
16∫0πsin⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=4sin⁡(2θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(4sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=8∫θ1θ2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 4sin⁡(2θ)=0.

This gives us two solutions for 2θ∈[0,2π): 2θ=0,π⟹θ=0,π2

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[0,π2]. Notice that this interval lies in the first quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

A=8∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

q-127800.name: Question 6
q-127800.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/446278a820ba21da7f5a1f15639e8cc4f96e38f38f3b5905b926bb9d2a106948.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-127800.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $6\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
6\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{12}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{12},\frac{\pi }{12}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /12}^{\pi /12}{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-127800.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=22cos⁡(6θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
4∫−π/12π/12cos⁡(6θ)dθ
b
14∫−π/12π/12cos2⁡(6θ)dθ
c
12∫−π/12π/12cos⁡(6θ)dθ
d
12∫−π/12π/12cos2⁡(6θ)dθ
e
2∫−π/12π/12cos2⁡(6θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=22cos⁡(6θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(22cos⁡(6θ))2dθ=14∫θ1θ2cos2⁡(6θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 22cos⁡(6θ)=0.

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that θ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for 6θ∈[−π,π): 6θ=−π2,π2⟹θ=−π12,π12

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π12,π12]. Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

14∫−π/12π/12cos2⁡(6θ)dθ.

q-83792.name: Question 7
q-83792.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/f3196a19057d5a5f658faad1ef028b12a12b87de56f93dc3f2df1aa03f21fcf2.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-83792.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $7\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
7\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{14},\frac{\pi }{14}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{14},\frac{\pi }{14}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /14}^{\pi /14}{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-83792.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(7θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
2∫−π/7π/7cos2⁡(7θ)dθ
b
14∫−π/14π/14cos2⁡(7θ)dθ
c
∫−π/14π/14cos2⁡(7θ)dθ
d
∫0π/14cos2⁡(7θ)dθ
e
12∫0π/14cos2⁡(7θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=2cos⁡(7θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(2cos⁡(7θ))2dθ=∫θ1θ2cos2⁡(7θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 2cos⁡(7θ)=0.

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that θ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for 7θ∈[−π,π):

7θ=−π2,π2⟹θ=−π14,π14

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π14,π14]. Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

∫−π/14π/14cos2⁡(7θ)dθ.

q-124423.name: Question 8
q-124423.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/1c296052cfe60b35b326029afa1efb610ce32e4e2fb3ae0d63f24e437c3bbfb2.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-124423.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $3\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
3\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-124423.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(3θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
∫−π/6πcos2⁡(3+θ)dθ
b
∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
c
∫−π/6π/6cos⁡(3θ)dθ
d
14∫−π/6π/2cos2⁡(3θ)dθ
e
12∫0π/6cos2⁡(θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=2cos⁡(3θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(2cos⁡(3θ))2dθ=∫θ1θ2cos2⁡(3θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 2cos⁡(3θ)=0.

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that θ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for 3θ∈[−π,π): 3θ=−π2,π2⟹θ=−π6,π6

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π6,π6]. Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

∫−π/6π/6cos2⁡(3θ)dθ.

q-124414.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/51ab11405aeb635dafaeadef1b174db163f395a62126225f99de07884b3d8cb9.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-124414.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $4\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
4\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{\pi }{8}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
2{\int }_{-\pi /8}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-124414.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=2cos⁡(4θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
12∫0π/8cos2⁡(θ)dθ
b
 2∫−π/8π/8cos⁡(4θ)dθ
c
 2∫−π/8π/8cos2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
 ∫0πcos2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
 14∫0π/4cos2⁡(4+θ)dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=2cos⁡(4θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ=2∫θ1θ2cos2⁡(4θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 2cos⁡(4θ)=0. Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that θ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for 4θ∈[−π,π):

4θ=−π2,π2⟹θ=−π8,π8

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π8,π8]. Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

2∫−π/8π/8cos2⁡(4θ)dθ.

q-14916.name: Question 10
q-14916.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/f62e6a4cec5b2a877f2491a101f3929edd6664424b86daab4bbfe8096c5c9282.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ),$ represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-14916.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\theta )=0.
$$

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that $\theta $ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for $5\theta \in [-\pi ,\pi ):$

$$
5\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{10},\frac{\pi }{10}
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for $\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{10},\frac{\pi }{10}].$ Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /10}^{\pi /10}{cos}^{2}⁡(5\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-14916.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=3cos⁡(5θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
92∫−π/5π/5cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
b
29∫−π/2π/2cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
c
32∫0π/10cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
d
92∫−π/10π/10cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
e
23∫0π/2cos2⁡(5θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=3cos⁡(5θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(3cos⁡(5θ))2dθ=92∫θ1θ2cos2⁡(5θ)dθ.

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 3cos⁡(5θ)=0.

Notice that the first petal lies between the first and fourth quadrants. So it's convenient to assume that θ can be negative.

We now solve the above equation for 5θ∈[−π,π): 5θ=−π2,π2⟹θ=−π10,π10

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π10,π10]. Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

92∫−π/10π/10cos2⁡(5θ)dθ.

q-125349.name: Question 11
q-125349.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/9405ee6a4b24ef36c2a59a9f4a984728716e9c281456d1459d591393d3c73720.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve
$r=\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )},$
  represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-125349.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )} & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal lies in the fourth quadrant. Since the petal lies in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $4\theta +\pi $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
4\theta +\pi =-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,4\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{2},-\frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{3\pi }{8},-\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{3\pi }{8},-\frac{\pi }{8}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies in the fourth quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3\pi /8}^{-\pi /8}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\pi )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-125349.html:
Question 11
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=cos⁡(4θ+π), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
12∫−3π/8−π/8cos2⁡(4θ+π)dθ
b
12∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡(4θ+π)dθ
c
12∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡(4θ+π)dθ
d
12∫−3π/8−π/8cos⁡(4θ+π)dθ
e
12∫−3π/83π/8cos⁡(4θ+π)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=cos⁡(4θ+π), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2cos⁡(4θ+π)dθ

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or cos⁡(4θ+π)=0cos⁡(4θ+π)=0.

From the diagram, the first petal lies in the fourth quadrant. Since the petal lies in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of θ when determining the interval.

The solutions for 4θ+π closest to 0 on either side are

4θ+π=−π2,π2⟹4θ=−3π2,−π2⟹θ=−3π8,−π8.

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for

θ∈[−3π8,−π8].

Notice that this interval lies in the fourth quadrant, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

12∫−3π/8−π/8cos⁡(4θ+π)dθ.

q-127997.name: Question 12
q-127997.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/0befc6c40eb7b53a45f1e27d0445d5abc614937c37b36d5cbf5420e1d2b51ff9.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve 
$r=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ),$
 represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-127997.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $4\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
4\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{24},\frac{5\pi }{24}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{5\pi }{24},\frac{5\pi }{24}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /24}^{5\pi /24}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-127997.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=3+2cos⁡(4θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
12∫−5π/245π/24(3+2cos⁡(4θ))dθ
b
12∫−5π/125π/12(3+2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ
c
12∫−5π/65π/6(3+2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ
d
12∫−5π/245π/24(3+2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ
e
12∫−5π/65π/6(3+2cos⁡(4θ))dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=3+2cos⁡(4θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(3+2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 3+2cos⁡(4θ)=02cos⁡(4θ)=−3cos⁡(4θ)=−32.

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of θ when determining the interval.

The solutions for 4θ closest to 0 on either side are

4θ=−5π6,5π6⟹θ=−5π24,5π24.

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for

θ∈[−5π24,5π24].

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

12∫−5π/245π/24(3+2cos⁡(4θ))2dθ.

q-128009.name: Question 13
q-128009.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/cc41b37639eb7715fbecd55510222f77957c05b705bc83b93c755ad2e7cf3dcd.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve
$r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}),$
  represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-128009.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}$ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}=-\pi ,\pi \,⟹\,4\theta =-\frac{11\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{11\pi }{24},\frac{\pi }{24}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{11\pi }{24},\frac{\pi }{24}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-11\pi /24}^{\pi /24}{(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta +\frac{5\pi }{6}))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-128009.html:
Question 13
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
 12∫−13π/24π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))dθ
b
 12∫−11π/12π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))2dθ
c
 12∫−11π/24π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))2dθ
d
 12∫−15π/24π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))2dθ
e
 12∫−11π/24π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))2dθ

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6)=0cos⁡(4θ+5π6)=−1.

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of θ when determining the interval.

The solutions for 4θ+5π6 closest to 0 on either side are 4θ+5π6=−π,π⟹4θ=−11π6,π6⟹θ=−11π24,π24.

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for

θ∈[−11π24,π24].

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

12∫−11π/24π/24(1+cos⁡(4θ+5π6))2dθ.

q-360575.name: Question 14
q-360575.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/6feb80156311c92f948b35742b39df3e6582c62a0d578481026b3141b01de3f1.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve 
$r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$
 represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-360575.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $6\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
6\theta =-\pi ,\pi \,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{6}].
$$

Notice that this interval matches the angular region traced by the shaded petal in the diagram.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-360575.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=2+2cos⁡(6θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
 ∫−π/8π/8(2+2cos⁡(6θ))dθ
b
 12∫−π/8π/8(2+2cos⁡(6θ))2dθ
c
 12∫−π/12π/12(2+2cos⁡(6θ))2dθ
d
 12∫−π/6π/6(2+2cos⁡(6θ))2dθ
e
 ∫−π/6π/6(2+2cos⁡(6θ))dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=2+2cos⁡(6θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(2+2cos⁡(6θ))2dθ

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 2+2cos⁡(6θ)=0cos⁡(6θ)=−1.

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of θ when determining the interval.

The solutions for 6θ closest to 0 on either side are 6θ=−π,π⟹θ=−π6,π6.

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for θ∈[−π6,π6].

Notice that this interval matches the angular region traced by the shaded petal in the diagram.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

12∫−π/6π/6(2+2cos⁡(6θ))2dθ.

q-125357.name: Question 15
q-125357.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226023/assets/d9985c6afd3e5440dbe1e51e4046e7744c9a2e01472354054796247d40ed7ed6.png)

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve 
$r=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),$
represented by the shaded region shown above?
q-125357.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r(\theta )=\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the integration limits. 

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of $\theta $ for which $r=0$, or 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of $\theta $ when determining the interval.

The solutions for $2\theta $ closest to $0$ on either side are

$$
2\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{5\pi }{6}\,⟹\,\theta =-\frac{5\pi }{12},\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for 

$$
\theta \in [-\frac{5\pi }{12},\frac{5\pi }{12}].
$$

 

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-5\pi /12}^{5\pi /12}{(\sqrt{3}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

q-125357.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following represents the area enclosed by the first petal of the polar curve r=3+2cos⁡(2θ), represented by the shaded region shown above?

a
12∫−π/12π/12(3+2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
b
12∫−5π/125π/12(3+2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
c
12∫−5π/65π/6(3+2cos⁡(2θ))dθ
d
12∫−5π/65π/6(3+2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
e
12∫−5π/125π/12(3+2cos⁡(2θ))dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

Since r(θ)=3+2cos⁡(2θ), we obtain

A=12∫θ1θ2(3+2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ

We now proceed to find the integration limits.

The curve bounding the region crosses itself at the origin. Therefore, we want to find the values of θ for which r=0, or 3+2cos⁡(2θ)=02cos⁡(2θ)=−3cos⁡(2θ)=−32.

From the diagram, the first petal extends from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant. Since the petal begins in the fourth quadrant, it is convenient to allow negative values of θ when determining the interval.

The solutions for 2θ closest to 0 on either side are

2θ=−5π6,5π6⟹θ=−5π12,5π12.

Therefore, the first petal is traversed for

θ∈[−5π12,5π12].

Notice that this interval lies between the first and fourth quadrants, the same as our petal.

Therefore, our expression for the area is given by

12∫−5π/125π/12(3+2cos⁡(2θ))2dθ.
